subject: Animation
title: The Armature: Skeleton of a Puppet
description: A quick, practical guide to The Armature: Skeleton of a Puppet.

hook.text: Every stop-motion puppet hides a secret inside: a precision-engineered metal skeleton called an armature.

buildup.text: Armatures use tiny ball-and-socket joints that hold any position an animator places them in.

discovery.text: A well-built armature lets an animator move a puppet in fractions of millimeters with total control.

twist.text: Professional armatures can cost thousands of dollars each and take weeks to machine by hand.

climax.text: The armature is invisible to the audience, but without it, no stop-motion puppet could hold a pose.

punchline.text: A hidden metal skeleton gives puppets the gift of stillness.

quiz.question: What is an armature in stop-motion animation?
options: A type of camera used for filming
A precision-engineered metal skeleton inside a puppet that holds poses
The background set of a stop-motion scene

details.summary: The armature is the internal metal skeleton of a stop-motion puppet, made from precision ball-and-socket joints. It must hold any pose yet move smoothly, making it the most critical engineering component in puppet animation.
details.whyItMatters: A bad armature ruins every frame. The quality of stop-motion animation depends fundamentally on armature engineering, making puppet builders as essential as the animators themselves.
takeaways: Armatures are precision metal skeletons inside stop-motion puppets
Ball-and-socket joints allow smooth positioning and pose-holding
Armature quality directly determines animation quality

faq.question: What materials are armatures made from?
faq.answer: Professional armatures use stainless steel or brass ball-and-socket joints connected by machined metal bars. The joints must be tight enough to hold a pose under the puppet's weight but loose enough to adjust smoothly.

faq.question: What happens when an armature fails during production?
faq.answer: Metal fatigue can cause joints to break mid-scene, potentially ruining weeks of animation. Studios keep backup puppets and carefully track joint wear. Some productions lose entire sequences to armature failure.
